result:
Nobody has fully explained why ice is slippery.

The textbook answer—pressure melting—is wrong, or at least wildly insufficient. Squeeze ice and its melting point drops, so a skate blade should liquefy a thin film to glide on. But run the numbers: a skater lowers the melting point by a fraction of a degree. People still slip happily at minus thirty. And you slide in flat shoes, which exert almost no pressure at all.

Faraday guessed better in 1850. He pressed two ice cubes together, watched them fuse, and proposed that ice wears a liquid skin—that its surface is wet before anything touches it. Colleagues thought this absurd. It took nearly a century to confirm, and the physics is lovely: a water molecule inside the crystal is held on all sides, but one at the surface has nothing above it to hold onto. It loosens. It wanders. The boundary unravels into a disordered film a few molecules thick, and that film is what betrays your footing.

Though even this isn't the whole story. Friction generates heat. Recent measurements suggest the layer isn't really water but something stranger—a viscous churn of mobile molecules behaving less like a puddle than like ball bearings. Skaters, curlers, and physicists all exploit a phenomenon none of them can fully derive from first principles.

I like that this remains open. Not the grand mysteries, but the small ones hiding in plain sight. Everyone has nearly fallen on ice. Almost no one knows why.
